A: Fundus photograph of the left eye in a child with ocular ischemic syndrome, showing vitreous hemorrhage, optic disc pallor, arteriolar narrowing, and midperipheral dot-blot hemorrhages. B: Early-phase fluorescein angiogram of the left eye showing delayed choroidal filling and arteriolar narrowing, consistent with ocular ischemic syndrome. C: Late-phase fluorescein angiogram of the left eye demonstrating peripheral abnormal arteriovenous communications and staining, as seen in ocular ischemic syndrome. D: Optical coherence tomography of the left eye showing retinal atrophy and ganglion cell layer thinning in ocular ischemic syndrome.

Optical coherence tomography (D) demonstrates moderate diffuse retinal atrophy, severe ganglion cell layer thinning, and mild vitreous opacities.

panels.rationale: Single-panel fundus fluorescein angiogram of the left eye from a case report whose diagnosis is ocular ischemic syndrome; the caption documents left optic disc hyper-fluorescence (arrowed), and the article title attributes the presentation to optic disc neovascularization as the only sign of ocular ischemic syndrome. The manifestation (disc neovascularization/hyperfluorescence) is a recognized OIS finding in the provided vocabulary. Disc hyperfluorescence itself is non-specific, hence moderate confidence; no skin, ethnicity or age data are given in the caption.

in_text_mentions: The patient underwent fundus fluorescein angiography that showed hyper-fluorescence on the left optic disc with no areas of capillary dropout (Figure 2). Accordingly, an urgent MRI of both orbits was arranged for the exclusion of compressive left optic neuropathy. The MRI, however, did not show any significant findings. Due to the suspicion of ocular ischemic syndrome, she had carotid Doppler to rule out carotid artery occlusion.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Right-eye fundus fluorescein angiogram in a patient with ocular ischemic syndrome; in-text reports prolonged choroidal filling time, a specific OIS angiographic manifestation. in_text_mentions: The glaucoma service was consulted, and the patient received 3 rounds of timolol, dorzolamide, and brimonidine in the right eye and 500 mg oral acetazolamide; the IOP improved to 16 mmHg 2 hours later. The retina service was consulted, and fluorescein angiography demonstrated profound peripheral retinal non-perfusion in both eyes with no NVD or NVE (Figure 2). The patient was diagnosed with open-angle NVG secondary to OIS in the right eye and underwent prompt intravitreal injection with 1.25 mg (0.05 ml) bevacizumab (IVB) that day.

A: Panel A shows iris neovascularization, a recognized clinical manifestation of Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS), indicated by the white arrow. B: Panel B shows Retinal Artery Occlusion (RAO) (red arrow) and cotton wool spots (blue arrow), both characteristic features of Ocular Ischemic Syndrome. C: Panel C shows pale optic disc/retina and RAO, consistent with the ischemic features of Ocular Ischemic Syndrome. D: Panel D shows cotton wool spots in the fundus, a finding associated with Ocular Ischemic Syndrome.
